In his farewell speech, Wendell Prusak uses personal stories and plain, specific details to make his students believe that being reliable and noticing small things matter. Because he is only a bus driver and not a teacher or principal, he has to earn the audience's attention, and he does it by sounding honest and humble instead of giving orders.

Prusak starts with the story of being told to be at Pell Road and the old creamery at 6:52. He says "Not 6:50. Not 6:55. Six fifty-two." The short repeated sentences make the time feel important, and the exact number shows how much he cared about it. This works on students because it makes the idea of a promise into a real person, a girl named Tansy with her clarinet case who would "stand in the dark thinking nobody was coming." Even the younger kids can understand that feeling. He also says "A bus route is a promise," which gives a simple definition that the whole speech can build on. Later he admits that Route 9 broke the promise "eleven times," and that he remembers the reason for each one. This makes him seem trustworthy because he does not pretend to be perfect.

In the middle of the speech Prusak describes the road and the things he sees, like the leaning mailbox and the heron "like a man waiting for a bus of his own." He repeats "I know" over and over, which shows how much attention he has paid. The line "Small things are not small. They are just quiet" is easy to remember and sums up his message. Then he deals with the students' doubts by saying "the heron will not get you into college." By admitting this, he shows he understands that students have tests and phones and pressure, so they are more likely to keep listening instead of thinking he is just an old man lecturing them.

The story of the black ice is where the tone gets more serious. He says the ditch "saw me," and that Augie told him "You did good, Mr. Prusak." Prusak says he did not do good, he got lucky. This shows he is willing to be humble in front of the students, and it also shows that noticing goes both ways, since a seven-year-old noticed him. That makes his message feel real instead of just advice.

At the end he gives simple commands like "Show up when you said you would" and "Look out the window." He then brings back 6:52 when he tells them Ms. Oyelaran "will be at Pell Road at 6:52." This ties the speech together and passes the promise on to the new driver. Overall, Prusak persuades by being specific, honest, and humble, so his students will remember that showing up and paying attention are what matter.

Wendell Prusak gives a speech to the students at Garnet Hollow on the last day of school because he is retiring. He talks about being a bus driver for thirty-one years and he uses a lot of stories and details to make his point that keeping promises and noticing small things are important. This essay will show how he does that.

In the first paragraph he starts with a story about the first day he got the job. He says he was told to be at the corner at 6:52 and not 6:50 or 6:55. This is a good way to start because it gets the audience interested and it shows how exact he was. The girl Tansy with the clarinet is also an example that makes the students feel something. He says he has thought about her every morning, which shows he cared about his riders.

Next he says a bus route is a promise. This is a metaphor and it tells the students what he thinks. He also says the route broke the promise eleven times, which shows he is honest. Then he talks about the heron and the mailbox, and he says small things are not small, they are just quiet. This is a good line because it is easy to remember.

Later he tells about the day the bus almost crashed on the ice and a boy named Augie said "You did good, Mr. Prusak." This is a very emotional story and it makes the audience feel sad and happy. It shows that noticing goes both ways.

At the end he tells the students to show up and look out the window and he says the new driver Ms. Oyelaran will be at Pell Road at 6:52. This is a good ending because it goes back to the beginning. Overall Prusak uses stories and details to persuade the students, and it is effective because it makes them think about what he said.

When a bus driver stands up in front of the whole school, he doesn't have the authority of a principal or a commencement speaker. Wendell Prusak seems to know this. In his farewell talk, he doesn't build authority by claiming he did his job well. He builds it by remembering exactly, and by admitting where he failed. Through precise detail, a confession of his own failures, and a closing that brings back the 6:52 stop from his first sentence, Prusak convinces students from kindergarten to senior year that showing up and paying attention are really one habit, and he proves it by keeping a promise in the speech itself.

Prusak's first move is the time. He was told to be at Pell Road "by 6:52. Not 6:50. Not 6:55." A round number like "seven o'clock" would sound like a schedule, but 6:52 sounds like a person, and the next sentence explains why: a girl named Tansy would be standing there, and if the bus was early "she missed it," and if it was late "she stood in the dark thinking nobody was coming." The short fragments are simple enough for a kindergartner to follow, but they also show older students that the exact minute is about not leaving someone alone in the dark, not about rules. That sets up his metaphor, "A bus route is a promise." Then he admits Route 9 "has broken that promise eleven times." You would expect a retiring man to brag, but confessing a specific number makes him more believable than a perfect record would. Someone who counts his eleven failures obviously takes the promise seriously.

Next, Prusak turns to his second habit, noticing, and links it to the first. He says you'd think the road "goes gray on you, like wallpaper," and then flips it: "It does the opposite." The "I know" list that comes after (the leaning mailbox, the heron, the kid in the third row who "stopped talking in October") moves from objects to an animal to a person. The order matters, because it shows that noticing a mailbox is practice for noticing a classmate who is struggling. Only someone who drove the same seventeen miles every day could know these things, so the reliability he talked about in paragraph two is what makes the attention possible. His line "Small things are not small. They are just quiet" sounds like a riddle to little kids, and older students can take it as a real idea.

Prusak also knows teenagers might roll their eyes, so he says what they're thinking for them: "the heron will not get you into college. Fair enough." Because he grants their point first, his questions about "who do you want to be at fifty-eight?" come across as respectful instead of preachy. This concession earns him the right to tell the most personal story in the speech, the near-crash on the creamery curve. The tone drops, and the understatement "We stopped a foot short" lets the danger speak for itself. Then comes the reversal: seven-year-old Augie says "You did good, Mr. Prusak," and Prusak answers, "I did not do good. I got lucky." Once again his authority comes from honesty and not competence. The bigger point is that the child noticed the adult, so "the noticing runs both directions." That gives even the youngest kids in the gym a role. They aren't just passengers being watched over.

The ending brings everything together. His requests are small on purpose: "Show up," "Look out the window," "Learn one true thing." In paragraph two he promised to say something "smaller" than a safety lecture, and he kept that promise. Then he hands the route over: Ms. Oyelaran "will be at Pell Road at 6:52." The time from his very first sentence comes back, so the whole speech turns into a single kept promise. His retirement doesn't break the route's promise. It passes the promise to someone new, and when he tells students "Be there," they become part of keeping it.

When Wendell Prusak stands up in the gym on his last day, he has no real authority over anyone in the room. He isn't a teacher or the principal, and after today he isn't even their driver. So instead of lecturing, Prusak earns his audience's trust by admitting where he fell short and by being almost stubbornly exact. He uses the humble details of Route 9 to argue that showing up and paying attention are really the same habit, and by the end the speech itself turns into a promise he hands to Ms. Oyelaran.

Prusak opens with a time, not a lesson: "6:52. Not 6:50. Not 6:55." The fragments are so short they almost sound like a joke, but the next sentence shows why the minutes matter. If the bus came early, Tansy missed it, and if it came late "she stood in the dark thinking nobody was coming." A round number like seven o'clock would just be a schedule. 6:52 is one particular girl on one particular corner, so the precision itself becomes the proof that he cared. That sets up his metaphor, "A bus route is a promise," and the colon that lets the promise speak for itself: "somebody will come for you." Then he does something surprising for a retirement speech and admits that Route 9 "has broken that promise eleven times." Someone trying to look good would leave that out. But students have heard plenty of adults act like they're perfect, so a confession this exact makes him more believable, not less. He obviously kept track of his failures the same way he kept track of the clock.

The middle of the speech shifts from showing up to noticing, and Prusak gets there with the reversal "It does the opposite." He expects listeners to assume that a route driven for thirty-one years turns into "wallpaper." Then he overturns that with the repeated "I know" list: the leaning mailbox, the heron, "the kid in the third row who stopped talking in October." This catalog reaches his whole audience at once. A kindergartner can picture a one-legged bird "waiting for a bus of his own," while an older student might recognize themselves as the kid nobody asked about. The antithesis "Small things are not small. They are just quiet" sums up the list in words short enough for a five-year-old to remember. Prusak also knows the seniors in the back are rolling their eyes, so he admits that "the heron will not get you into college." Because he grants their point instead of brushing it off, he earns the chance to ask his paired questions about who they want to be "at fifty-eight." His answer, "I don't think you have to choose," ties his two habits together into one.

That concession earns him the right to tell his most personal story. He tells the near-crash with understatement ("We stopped a foot short"), and he personifies the ditch as if it "saw me." That makes the danger feel real without scaring the little kids. The key line is "I did not do good. I got lucky." Once again he builds authority by confessing instead of bragging. And in this story the roles flip: seven-year-old Augie is the one who notices the driver. Prusak realizes that "the noticing runs both directions," which tells even the youngest students that their attention matters to adults too.

The ending pays off everything before it. In paragraph two Prusak promised to say something "smaller" than a safety speech, and his final requests really are small: "Show up," "Look out the window," learn "one true thing." Then 6:52 and Pell Road come back, only now they belong to Ms. Oyelaran. The speech's first sentence was about a promise made to Tansy, and its last is that same promise being passed on. Prusak doesn't just tell students that reliability matters. He shows that a promise kept long enough outlasts the person who made it, which is "the entire meaning of a morning."

Most retirement speeches are about the person retiring. Wendell Prusak's is mostly about a girl with a clarinet case, a heron in a ditch, and a seven-year-old who told him he did good. Prusak is talking to a gym full of kids from kindergarten to twelfth grade, and a bus driver has no real authority over any of them except the fact that he showed up. He makes that his whole argument. By rooting big ideas in exact, almost stubborn details, by building his credibility out of failures he admits instead of achievements he claims, and by ending where he started, at Pell Road at 6:52, Prusak makes the speech itself an example of the two habits he wants students to take on, and he passes that promise to his successor instead of just describing it.

Prusak's precision is his first argument. He doesn't say he picked kids up early in the morning. He says "6:52. Not 6:50. Not 6:55." The short fragments sound almost like a correction, as if someone once tried to round it off and he wouldn't let them. A round number would just be a schedule, but 6:52 belongs to a person, Tansy, who "stood in the dark thinking nobody was coming" if he was late. The youngest kids in the gym can picture that, and the older ones can see that being early would let her down too, which turns reliability into a way of caring about someone and not just obeying a clock. Then he says it straight out, "A bus route is a promise," and uses the colon to let the route talk: "somebody will come for you." A kindergartner hears a bus. A senior about to leave home hears what adults are supposed to owe each other. The "I know" list in paragraph 3 works the same way. It moves from a mailbox to a heron to "the kid in the third row who stopped talking in October," so by the end, noticing has gone from objects to people. When he says "Small things are not small. They are just quiet," the line sounds like something you'd remember, but it only works because he has already shown us three quiet things.

What makes the students trust him is that he keeps admitting things. He says Route 9 broke its promise "eleven times," when he could easily have said "almost never." Remembering the reason for every one of them proves the attention he is asking for. In paragraph 4 he says his audience's objection out loud before they can: "the heron will not get you into college. Fair enough." That respects the teenagers who might be rolling their eyes. The question "who do you want to be at fifty-eight?" is pointed, because he is fifty-eight, so he is offering himself as the answer, and "I don't think you have to choose" gets rid of the either/or he just set up. That honesty is what lets him tell the scariest story last. With the near-crash he goes quiet and understated: "the ditch saw me," "We stopped a foot short." Then he turns down Augie's compliment: "I did not do good. I got lucky." A driver bragging about saving the bus would sound like a safety lecture. A driver admitting luck sounds like the truth. The real point of the story is that the boy noticed him, so "the noticing runs both directions." Even the smallest kids in the room are being told they can do this too.

The ending keeps the promise from paragraph 2. He said he would say something "smaller" than a safety speech, and his requests really are small: "Show up when you said you would. Look out the window." Then 6:52 comes back, now with Ms. Oyelaran's name attached. "Be there" is the only order in the speech that sounds like an order, and it moves the promise from his route to the students. His retirement could have felt like something ending, but because the time stays the same, the route keeps going without him. In a way the speech is the last stop he makes on time.

In his farewell speech, Wendell Prusak persuades the students of Garnet Hollow that being reliable and noticing small things matter by building the speech out of personal stories and plain, specific details instead of lectures. Because he is only a bus driver and not a teacher or principal, he has to earn the students' attention, and he does this by sounding honest and humble.

He starts with the story of being told to be at Pell Road at "6:52. Not 6:50. Not 6:55." The exact time makes the promise feel real, since a round number would sound careless. The short repeated fragments also sound like the way a boss would give orders, so the audience can hear how strict the job was. Then he brings in Tansy, the girl with the clarinet, which makes the time about a person instead of a schedule. This works on younger students because it is a story, and older students can see the point too. He also says "I have thought about that girl almost every morning since," which shows that he took the promise seriously.

Prusak also builds trust by admitting his faults. He says the route "has broken that promise eleven times" and that he knows the reason for every one. Instead of bragging that he was perfect, he gives a number, which makes him seem believable. Later he tells the story of the ice on the creamery curve where "the ditch saw me." This personification makes the danger feel scary, and then he says "We stopped a foot short," which is understated. When the little boy Augie says "You did good," Prusak says "I did not do good." This shows he is humble and also shows that the students noticed him back. It matters to the students because it shows even a seven-year-old can matter to an adult.

Another choice is that he answers the students' doubts. In the fourth paragraph he admits "the heron will not get you into college," and then asks two questions about who they want to be at fifty-eight. By admitting the objection first, he seems fair, and the questions make the students think for themselves instead of being told. This helps the audience of teenagers who are busy with tests and phones.

Finally, the ending brings back the time, "Ms. Oyelaran, and she will be at Pell Road at 6:52." This ties the speech together and hands the job to the new driver. His short commands, "Show up when you said you would. Look out the window," are easy to remember. Overall, Prusak uses stories, honesty, and repetition to make his small message feel important, and since it is his last day, the students are more likely to listen.

In his farewell speech, Wendell Prusak persuades the students of Garnet Hollow that reliability and paying attention are worth building a life around by using small, personal stories instead of big advice. Because he is only a bus driver and not a teacher or principal, he earns the audience's trust by being specific, honest about his mistakes, and by treating the students as people who might doubt him.

Prusak starts with the story of Tansy and the 6:52 stop. He says the bus had to come at "Not 6:50. Not 6:55. Six fifty-two." The short repeated fragments make the time sound strict, almost like a rule, and the odd exact time shows how seriously he took it. By saying that if the bus came early she missed it and if it came late she thought "nobody was coming," he shows that being on time is really about caring for another person. This is a good way to start with students because even the younger ones can understand a girl waiting alone in the dark, and it makes his point without lecturing.

Next, he says "A bus route is a promise." This is a metaphor that takes something the students see every day and gives it a bigger meaning. He then admits that Route 9 broke the promise "eleven times" and that he remembers each reason. Admitting this makes him seem more believable, since he is not pretending to be perfect. The students are more likely to listen to someone honest about failing than someone bragging.

In the middle of the speech he turns to noticing small things. He compares the road to wallpaper but says "It does the opposite," and then lists things he knows, like the leaning mailbox and the heron. The repeated "I know" shows how much he has paid attention. Then he admits the students might think "the heron will not get you into college." This concession shows he understands their pressures, especially the older students, and so they may be more willing to accept his question about who they want to be at fifty-eight.

The near-crash story in paragraph five is the emotional high point. He says the ditch "saw me," which makes the danger feel alive, and the understatement "We stopped a foot short" keeps it calm. When Augie says "You did good," and Prusak says he did not, it shows he is humble. It also shows noticing goes both ways, which supports his message.

Finally, he ends with simple commands, "Show up when you said you would. Look out the window," and brings back 6:52 when he tells them the new driver Ms. Oyelaran will be at Pell Road. This hands the promise on to her and makes the students feel they can trust her. Overall, Prusak uses stories, honesty, and repetition to make a plain job seem like a model for how to live.

A retiring bus driver has no real power over the students sitting in that gym. He can't give out grades, and in a few hours he won't even be their driver anymore. So when Wendell Prusak tries to convince everyone from kindergartners to seniors that showing up and paying attention are what a good life is made of, he can't rely on authority. Instead, Prusak builds his credibility out of exact details and admitted failures, and he ends his speech back at the 6:52 stop so that his whole thirty-one years turn into one promise that he is passing on to someone else.

Prusak defines what a promise is before he ever uses the word. He tells the students the stop was at 6:52, "Not 6:50. Not 6:55." The fragments make the listener notice how small the window is. A round number like "around seven" would sound like a schedule, but 6:52 sounds like a person, and he gives her a name: Tansy, with her clarinet case. If the bus was late she "stood in the dark thinking nobody was coming." Even a five-year-old knows what it feels like to wait and think nobody is coming, so being late stops being a rule about timing and becomes something that hurts a person. When he finally says "A bus route is a promise," the audience has already felt it. Then he admits that Route 9 broke that promise "eleven times." That's an odd thing to say at your own retirement, since farewells are usually about celebrating. But the confession is what makes the other thirty-one years believable. High schoolers who are tired of adults lecturing them will trust a man who keeps count of his failures more than a man who brags.

The second habit, noticing, works the same way. Prusak sets up what students would expect, that the road "goes gray on you, like wallpaper," and then reverses it: "It does the opposite." The repeated "I know" moves from a mailbox to a heron to "the kid in the third row who stopped talking in October," so the list goes from objects to animals to people and the stakes go up with it. He even describes the heron as "a man waiting for a bus of his own," which shows that his noticing is filtered through his job. The two habits aren't separate for him. The line "Small things are not small. They are just quiet" is short enough for little kids to remember, but the older students can see that he isn't saying small things are secretly big, just that nobody announces them.

The concession in paragraph four is aimed right at the teenagers. He puts their objection in their own words, "tests, and phones," and admits "the heron will not get you into college." Saying "Fair enough" lets the skeptics feel heard before he asks "who do you want to be at fifty-eight?" Giving up that point is what earns him the near-crash story that comes next. He already admitted that noticing doesn't help your transcript, so now he shows a moment when it mattered more than anything. The personification "the ditch saw me" and the understatement "We stopped a foot short" keep the story calm instead of dramatic, and once again he refuses credit: "I did not do good. I got lucky." The important part is that seven-year-old Augie is the one who notices him. This reversal tells every kid in the gym that they already know how to do what he's asking, because a second grader did it on his bus.

That is why the ending feels earned. The imperatives "Show up" and "Look out the window" really are "smaller" than a safety speech, just like he promised in paragraph two, so the speech keeps its own promise. Then 6:52 and Pell Road come back with Ms. Oyelaran. The stop that started with Tansy now belongs to someone new, and "Be there" asks the students to keep their side of the deal. Prusak's retirement isn't really an ending. It is the promise being handed over, still on time.
